summary:
Saint Kitts and Nevis no longer criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. In 2022 the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court, in Jamal Jeffers v The Attorney General, struck section 56 (buggery) and section 57 (indecent assault against a man) of the Offences Against the Person Act as contrary to the rights to privacy and expression. Consensual same-sex conduct has been lawful throughout the country since that ruling.

Legal gender recognition is not possible in Saint Kitts and Nevis. A person cannot obtain official recognition of a changed gender marker, and the sources document no administrative route, court process or statute that would allow it.

No provision of the penal code or of any other statute prohibits discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Discrimination in the workplace, in education and in accommodation remains lawful, as does hate speech, and no anti-discrimination statute has been enacted in the years since decriminalisation.

Relationship recognition is absent in full. Same-sex unions are not recognised in any form, whether marriage or partnership, and same-sex households receive none of the rights granted to opposite-sex married couples.

The protection machinery that does exist sits in policy rather than law. LGBTQ+ citizens are included in the National Gender Equality Policy 2022-2027, but a 2025 joint presentation to the Universal Periodic Review by the Saint Kitts and Nevis Alliance and ECADE records a lack of tangible steps by the State to implement that inclusion.

Relations with the authorities are a separate matter from the statute book. The same 2025 submission states that LGBTQ+ people avoid law enforcement, which bears directly on whether a visitor can expect assistance if a bias-motivated incident occurs. LGBTI organisations are permitted to register, and civil society used the courts rather than the legislature to obtain decriminalisation.

The practical position for a trans visitor is therefore lawful private conduct without protective scaffolding: conduct between adults is not an offence, but there is no anti-discrimination law, no recognised gender marker, no recognised relationship, and no sourced evidence of state remedies being used after a bias incident.
tangentialFactors:
Decriminalisation in Saint Kitts and Nevis arrived through a regional wave of constitutional litigation rather than legislative reform. Human Dignity Trust documents Eastern Caribbean challenges to anti-sodomy laws, and the August 2022 Nation News report covers the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court striking down such laws across several territories in the same judgment family, with Jamal Jeffers v Attorney General the case that applies to Saint Kitts and Nevis.

The pattern is regional and litigation-driven. Outlets tracking these statutes report ongoing lawsuits against several Caribbean nations over anti-gay laws and frame courts as the principal mechanism for expanding LGBTQ rights in the Caribbean, which indicates that the current legal position rests on a judicial ruling that a future legislature or court could in principle revisit.

Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, records the same three findings as the domestic submissions: consensual same-sex conduct legal since 2022, legal gender recognition not available, and LGBTI organisations free to register. Independent trackers of anti-gay laws list no post-repeal discrimination statute for Saint Kitts and Nevis, consistent with the Universal Periodic Review submission.
localsOnly:
Residents have no legal means of changing a gender marker, so identity documents, employment records and civil status documents all remain aligned to sex assigned at birth with no statutory correction procedure.

Same-sex couples have no marital or partnership status and no inheritance, next-of-kin, tax or social-protection entitlements flowing from a recognised relationship. Cohabitation confers none of the rights attached to opposite-sex marriage.

Employment, education and housing discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is lawful, as is hate speech, leaving residents without a statutory complaint route in those settings. The National Gender Equality Policy 2022-2027 names LGBTQ+ citizens as within its scope, but the Saint Kitts and Nevis Alliance and ECADE report that the State has not taken tangible implementing steps.

LGBTQ+ people avoid law enforcement, which affects reporting of domestic violence, assault and harassment by residents as much as visitors. LGBTI organisations may register and operate, and the 2022 challenge to the Offences Against the Person Act was brought by civil society, demonstrating a functioning route to the courts for constitutional claims.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records incidents of violence against trans people in Saint Kitts and Nevis, their frequency, dates, police response or judicial outcome. Absence of documented cases should be read as unsourced rather than as evidence that no such violence occurs.

Entry and border screening are not addressed by any source here: whether immigration officers question travellers whose passports carry amended gender markers, or require supporting documentation, remains unresolved from this material.

Hate-crime enhancement for bias-motivated assaults is not covered by the inventory. The sources establish that anti-discrimination and hate-speech conduct are not unlawful, which is not the same finding as whether a court would treat gender identity as an aggravating factor in sentencing.

Whether the Offences Against the Person Act or any other statute retains gendered or sex-based provisions that could reach a trans person in specific circumstances, such as public order or indecency offences, is not sourced and cannot be stated either way from this material.

The implementation record of the National Gender Equality Policy 2022-2027 is characterised in the 2025 Universal Periodic Review submission only as lacking tangible steps; no government response or subsequent evaluation was available to weigh against that assessment.
